reason: The sources reliably support a compelling 45-second script about the Brescia explosion with verified multi-source claims.
story: On August 18, 1769, a summer storm broke over the walled city of Brescia, Italy. At dawn, lightning struck the Bastion of San Nazaro, igniting 90 tons of Venetian gunpowder stored inside. The resulting cataclysm leveled one-sixth of the city, hurling massive stones across a kilometer radius and crushing homes and churches. While official records later counted hundreds dead, contemporary accounts and later histories claimed casualties soared into the thousands. The disaster exposed the deadly flaw of storing gunpowder inside urban areas and near churches, which people mistakenly believed were protected from lightning by divine intervention and ringing bells. The catastrophe horrified Europe and prompted Benjamin Franklin to successfully champion pointed lightning rods to tame the skies.
angle: A massive bolt of lightning struck a church bastion storing 90 tons of gunpowder because townspeople believed ringing church bells and divine intervention would protect them.

disputed: Death tolls vary significantly across sources: official reports from two years later state 400 dead, English sources often report 3,000, and French writer Louis-Sébastien Mercier claimed 2,500. The script should attribute these figures accordingly (e.g., 'official records noted 400, while later accounts claimed up to 3,000').

The claim that the Roman Catholic Church viewed lightning rods as heretical or relied on ringing church bells to ward off lightning is mentioned in select sources (S3, S4) as a widespread 18th-century superstition and practice; the script should attribute this belief as contemporary custom.
